newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan monopoly says raising oil prices 2.97 pct.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan monopoly says raising oil prices 2.97 pct.

text.p: Taiwan oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Friday it was raising domestic oil prices by an average 2.97 percent effective from April 5.

The increase, authorised in principle in December by the economic ministry, needed no further authorisation as it fell within a limit allowing price adjustments of three percent or less in any single month, a Chinese Petroleum spokesman said.
"The adjustment does not require government approval," spokesman Tsai Shan-lang said on state television.
The adjustment comes just three months after a major price increase that took effect on January 1, when Chinese Petroleum raised domestic oil prices by an average nine percent.
The state-run monopoly has said the increases were necessary to cope with budget shortfalls arising from the unexpectedly high prices of international crude in recent months.
In addition to the January price hikes, the economic ministry also authorised the oil monopoly to raise local oil prices further -- but by no more than three percent -- after three months.
Chinese Petroleum posted a pre-tax loss of T$486 million in February, well below a targeted pre-tax profit of T$1.538 billion.
The firm has an accumulated deficit of T$1.965 billion from July to February. Chinese Petroleum calculates earning results based on a fiscal year of July to June.
The company has blamed the deficit mainly on world oil prices that were far higher than expected, saying it would need a 14 percent oil price increase to eliminate its current deficit.
